sections.title: Start here: the general contractor that owns the whole chain
sections.read: A GC turns a permit into commissioned megawatts; this one owns its architect, its concrete and enclosure trades, an MEP arm and a developer.
ps: **The trade.** A {{general contractor}} holds the owner's construction contract, plans and sequences the job, hires and coordinates the trades, and carries schedule and safety responsibility. In a data hall the critical trades are electrical and mechanical; the GC decides how they overlap and when the building is ready for them.

**The model here.** Vertical integration — in-house architecture and engineering, a self-performed concrete company, an enclosure company, a mechanical-electrical self-perform arm, and a real-estate developer that assembles land and power — sold as design-build: one contract, one responsible party.

**Why a seller cares.** On a design-build campus the GC's engineers write the basis of design, its procurement team runs the bid for generators and chillers, and its self-perform crews install them. On a construction-management campus the owner furnishes the equipment and the GC coordinates a hundred subcontractors. This guide teaches which is which, what a data-centre ranking measures, how speed to power is built, and why land and local politics are now part of the GC's business.
**Not here.** Founding dates, executives and revenue stay in the dossier.

sections.title: Why a GC self-performs concrete, enclosure and MEP
ps: Most general contractors subcontract every trade and manage; a {{self-perform}} GC employs its own craft for the trades that drive the schedule. Concrete is first — foundations, slabs and tilt-up or precast walls are the critical path for the first months of a data hall — and a GC that owns a concrete company controls when the building is ready for the trades that follow.

Enclosure is second: a watertight shell lets electrical and mechanical rough-in start. Mechanical and electrical self-perform is the hardest to build and the most valuable, because those trades are where hyperscale schedules slip; a GC with its own MEP crews can promise sequence rather than negotiate it.

The limit is labour. Self-performed craft must be hired, trained and kept busy; when a marquee client doubles the size of a follow-on phase on the same timeline, the GC either has the crews or it loses the phase to a rival that does. The dossier records exactly that case.

sections.title: Speed to power: how a data hall is sequenced
ps: Owners pay for time to energised capacity. The sequence runs site and civil work, then foundations and shell, then the equipment yard — generators, {{switchgear}}, transformers — while the building's electrical and mechanical rough-in proceeds inside, then equipment set, then {{commissioning}} from Level 1 through the integrated systems test, then {{energization}}.

Three levers compress it. {{Offsite fabrication}} of power assemblies and chiller skids moves hours off the critical path; design-build removes the redesign cycle between an owner's engineer and a builder; and concurrent engineering lets foundations pour while the electrical design is still closing.

On this company's flagship AI job the record names 'more than 100 integrated power assemblies and more than 90 chillers' with 'significant off-site assembly' and an on-site concrete batch plant. Those are the speed levers applied to a liquid-cooled retrofit of a former bitcoin site.

sections.title: Converting a bitcoin site into an AI data centre
ps: A bitcoin mine has what an AI campus needs most — a grid interconnection and transformers — and almost nothing else it needs: no {{UPS}}, no redundant distribution, air cooling sized for cheap ASICs rather than {{liquid cooling}} for GPUs. Converting one means keeping the power entry and rebuilding everything downstream.

{{Rack power density}} drives the rebuild. Racks that drew 10–15 kW now draw past 100 kW, which pushes the design from air to liquid: chillers and {{CDU}}s instead of CRAH units, piping to every rack, and far more {{power module}}s per hall. The structure changes too — heavier floors for liquid-cooled racks and larger equipment yards.

The GC's contribution is sequencing a live site: new foundations and structural steel beside operating infrastructure, chiller skids set as they arrive, and a phased hand-over so the tenant takes capacity in tranches rather than all at once.

sections.title: Powered land: when the builder is also the developer
ps: A {{powered shell}} is a building with grid power and cooling capacity ready for a tenant's racks; {{powered land}} is a site with the interconnection, water and zoning secured but nothing built. Developers sell or lease both to hyperscalers and colocation operators who want to skip the years of entitlement.

A GC with a development affiliate can offer develop-design-build: assemble the land, win the rezoning and the utility agreement, design and build the shell, and lease it. The attraction is control of the whole timeline; the exposure is political. Rezoning a few hundred acres for a gigawatt campus is a public act, and the record here shows what happens when it goes wrong — a withdrawn campus and a moratorium in one city, an approval followed by a council wipe-out and a {{Sunshine Law}} suit in another.
For a seller the developer arm is a second door: it signs for substations and sometimes for generation and storage before a tenant is named.

sections.title: When the owner stops paying: liens and working capital
ps: A design-builder on a billion-dollar plant pays its subcontractors monthly and bills the owner for progress. If the owner suspends the project — a battery plant stopped at three-quarters complete when federal incentives looked uncertain — the builder is left holding the last months of unpaid work. The legal tool is a {{mechanic's lien}}: a claim against the property itself for the value of work performed, enforced by a foreclosure suit.

The scale of the exposure is the lesson, not the lawsuit. A private GC that pays every subcontractor from its own funds while it waits is lending the owner working capital; the amount sued for is only the unpaid tail of a much larger receivable.

sections.title: A GC's solar-and-storage unit: who it buys from and sells to
ps: Utility-scale solar and {{BESS}} are built under {{turnkey EPC}}: the contractor engineers the plant, procures modules, inverters and batteries, and builds it for a utility, an independent power producer or a financial sponsor. A general contractor entering this market brings craft labour and project controls but no supplier relationships; its first projects reveal which battery and inverter makers it chooses.

The twist here is the customer list: the unit names 'data center operators' among its targets, which suggests behind-the-meter storage at campuses the GC already builds. For a storage seller, a GC's energy unit is a new procurement channel whose first named award is the thing to watch.

sections.title: Flashcards
sections.read: Mechanisms only — no dates, names or revenue figures.

cards.q: Under which delivery model does the general contractor most often buy the major electrical and mechanical equipment itself?
cards.a: Design-build (and turnkey EPC): the GC holds design and procurement inside its price. Under construction management the owner furnishes it.

cards.q: Why does a GC self-perform concrete before any other trade?
cards.a: Foundations, slabs and walls are the critical path of a data hall's first months; owning the concrete crew controls when the building is ready for the trades that follow.

cards.q: What are the three levers that compress time to energised capacity?
cards.a: Offsite fabrication of power and cooling assemblies, design-build to remove the redesign cycle, and concurrent engineering so civil work proceeds while design closes.

cards.q: What does a bitcoin mine already have that an AI data centre needs, and what must be rebuilt?
cards.a: The grid interconnection and transformers; everything downstream — UPS, redundant distribution, liquid cooling, heavier structure — must be added.

cards.q: What does BD+C's data-centre contractor table rank on?
cards.a: Prior-year revenue the firm attributes to data-centre facilities, self-reported in a survey — not MW delivered or contract role.

cards.q: What is {{powered land}} and why does a GC want a developer affiliate?
cards.a: A site with interconnection, water and zoning secured; a developer affiliate lets the GC control the timeline from land to lease and signs for infrastructure before a tenant is named.
A claim against the property for the value of work performed, which a builder can foreclose when the owner stops paying.

items.q: An owner's engineer designs the data hall and the owner buys the generators and UPS; the GC coordinates a hundred subcontractors for a fee. Which model is this?
c: CM at risk with GC-furnished gear
items.why: Owner-held design, owner-furnished equipment and a coordination fee are agency construction management.

items.q: A client doubles the size of a follow-on phase on the same timeline and moves it to a rival GC, citing labour. Which capability was the binding constraint?
items.why: Schedule on a doubled phase is set by how many crews and superintendents the GC can field.

items.q: Which change most forces a bitcoin-site conversion from air to liquid cooling?
c: Rack power density rising past 100 kW
items.why: Air cannot remove the heat of 100 kW racks; liquid cooling with CDUs and chillers is required.

items.q: Two GCs are USD 10m apart on a self-reported data-centre revenue table. What can you conclude?
c: The higher one builds more megawatts
Little — the gap is inside survey noise
The lower one is a construction manager
items.why: The table measures self-reported revenue attributed to a building type; a USD 10m gap on billions is not a ranking difference.

items.q: Why is a GC's development affiliate politically exposed in a way the construction business is not?
c: Rezoning hundreds of acres is a public act that invites organised opposition
items.why: Entitlement is decided in council chambers and elections; a builder hired after entitlement avoids that stage.

items.q: A design-builder sues for USD 26m on a plant where it performed more than USD 1bn of work. What does the suit measure?
c: The unpaid tail after it paid subcontractors from its own funds
items.why: The lien covers unpaid progress billings; the working capital lent to the owner is the larger exposure.

glossary.d: The moment utility or generator power is applied to a facility's electrical system for the first time, after commissioning tests pass — the milestone data-centre owners schedule around.
A state open-meetings and open-records law; a suit alleging a council deliberated in private or gave inadequate notice can void the approval it produced.
A statutory claim a contractor or supplier records against real property for the value of unpaid work or materials, enforceable by foreclosure.
